items.title: ArcGIS Production Mapping Map Production System (MPS)
items.description:
ArcGIS Production Mappings Map Production System (MPS) application is a single access point for end users to create, manage, and prioritize map exports. MPS is designed to facilitate cartographic production by enabling batch map creation with predefined map layouts, symbology, and automatic cartographic refinement for the map production.

Key Features:

  • Create map product export types for visualization, print, and or map production.
  • Manage map product exports within your map production system.
items.snippet: Create, manage, and prioritize map exports for your map production.
items.licenseInfo:
• Map Production System application requires an ArcGIS Production Mapping Server License.
  • Map Production System application requires services that are published with a Topographic Production Capabilities.
  • Map Production System application requires an ArcGIS Production Mapping Server License.

items.title: Deep Learning Studio
items.description:
Deep Learning Studio provides a focused user experiences for users to extract information out of imagery and share it with your organization. The application allows you to perform an end-to-end workflow which includes capturing training data, training a model, and running inferencing. The application is flexible and allows you to perform individual steps when you have a custom workflow.

Key features:
With Deep Learning Studio you can:
  • Manage your deep learning projects with a focused user experience for object detection, pixel classification, or object classification.
  • Collaborate with your colleagues for collecting training samples and reviewing them.
  • Create and manage image chips from training samples or register existing image chips.
  • Train one or more iterations of your model with a guided user experience and compare training results.
  • Run inferencing based on the project or from Deep Learning Packages (DLPKs) available in your organization.
items.snippet: Easily manage the full life cycle of model development and use with Deep Learning Studio. This application provides an easy-to-use experience for collaborating preparing training data, training a deep learning model, and running inferencing against imagery.

items.title: ArcGIS AppStudio
items.description:
ArcGIS AppStudio is a groundbreaking tool in the GIS app revolution. For years, organizations have had to hire expensive third-party developers to build consumer-friendly GIS apps. Now, ArcGIS AppStudio puts the power back in your hands. It lets you convert your maps into beautiful, consumer-friendly mobile apps that you can share with the public through all popular app stores or securely within your own enterprise. Build an app once, and it is automatically ready for Android, iOS, Windows, OS X, and Linux.

To use your maps in AppStudio, you must have an ArcGIS organizational account. Your maps can include data from ArcGIS Online and ArcGIS for Server.

For more information, please visit http://appstudio.arcgis.com.

items.title: ArcGIS Tracker
items.description: Location tracking is an organization-wide capability, providing the ability to record where users are and where they have been. ArcGIS Tracker empowers location tracking, using the location tracking service in two apps: the Track Viewer web app and the ArcGIS Tracker mobile app available on iOS and Android. The Track Viewer web app allows administrators to create track views, defining which users have tracks included in the view and who can view those tracks. The Tracker mobile app is optimized for tracking locations in the background, minimizing the impact on device battery. The mobile app records tracks whether or not there is a data connection and gives mobile users control of when they are and aren't tracked.
items.snippet: ArcGIS Tracker empowers location tracking, using the location tracking service in two apps: the Track Viewer web app and the ArcGIS Tracker mobile app available on iOS and Android.

items.title: ArcGIS Indoors
items.description:
ArcGIS Indoors Web provides an indoor mapping experience for understanding the location of things and activities happening within your organization’s indoor environment. Use its capabilities to feel more connected to your workplace or campus, see increased levels of productivity and collaboration, and less time feeling the stress of being lost.

Key Features ArcGIS Indoors offers:

Navigation
With indoor navigation, you will always know where to go within your organization, where your colleagues and friends are, and where there is available space to meet your needs.

Explore and Search
With the ability to explore your organization and search for specific people, activities and events, offices and classrooms, and other points of interest, you will never have to wonder where something is located.

Calendar Integration
With calendar integration, see where your scheduled meetings are located and easily navigate between them knowing the estimated travel times and avoid being late for important events.

Events and Activities
With the ability see the time and location of events and activities in the map, you can make the most of your time and plan ahead for the distance to travel between them.

Save Favorites
Save locations to My Places to easily find your favorite people, events, or other points of interest again.

Location Sharing
With location sharing, you can make others aware of a specific location whether you’re coordinating an impromptu meetup, helping others locate an item, or reporting a problem.

311
Use the 311 capability to report incidents to your organization’s Information Systems or Facilities departments for issues with indoors assets or locations.
items.accessInformation: Use of the ArcGIS Indoors Web application requires a license for the ArcGIS Indoors organizational capability.

items.title: ArcGIS for Power BI
items.description:
ArcGIS for Power BI adds a new dimension to dashboards and reporting by providing all Power BI users with enhanced mapping and location analysis capabilities.  Using it is simple.  It ships in the box, so any Power BI user can just click on the icon and immediately start mapping.  Location-enable tabular business data, and then overlay it with curated global demographic data and basemaps for greater context.  Take your understanding even further by performing location analytics operations such as find nearby, find similar, and add infographic cards.

Core capabilities:

  • Map tabular business data:  Convert any tabular location value—an address, city, state, zip code, place name, boundary, or latitude and longitude to a map.  Visualize your data as points, areas, or clusters, and use the best background to let your data tell its story.
    •  
  • Get context:  Leverage curated ready-to-use map data, for perspective.  Select from hundreds of demographic and reference layers such as income, population, or weather for over 100 countries.  If your organization has ArcGIS, add your authoritative GIS data layers for context.
  • Accurate spatial analysis:  Make sense of your data by applying easy location analysis tools such as heat maps and drive times.  Spatial analysis quickly exposes relationships and patterns that can impact decision-making.

Get started with ArcGIS for Power BI

ArcGIS maps for Power BI is available to all Power BI Desktop and Power BI service (PowerBI.com) users at no cost.  Here’s how you get started:

  1. Sign in to Microsoft Power BI
  2. Create a new dashboard or open an existing one
  3. Within the Visualizations pane, click on the ArcGIS for Power BI icon
  4. Optional:  for more features and capabilities, sign up for the Plus subscription (no cost)
  5. Start mapping by dragging data from the Fields pane into Visualization field wells

ArcGIS for Power BI can also connect to your ArcGIS Online or ArcGIS Enterprise account, so you can access your organization’s authoritative GIS content.  Here’s how you get started:

  1. Ensure that an ArcGIS for Power BI license is assigned to your user account.  You may need to speak with your ArcGIS organizational administrator.
  2. Sign in to Microsoft Power BI
  3. Create a new dashboard or open an existing one
  4. Within the Visualizations pane, click on the ArcGIS for Power BI icon
  5. Sign into ArcGIS for Power BI with your ArcGIS Online or ArcGIS Enterprise credentials
  6. Start mapping by dragging data from the Fields pane into Visualization field wells

Find more about ArcGIS for Power BI.

Need Help? Visit our documentation page or contact us.

items.title: ArcGIS Mission Responder
items.description:
ArcGIS Mission Responder enables situational awareness for deployed team members during a mission and allows mobile users to work off the same designated map, provisioned to the device. Team members can send status and location updates and see each other’s positions in the field and share information with each other when connected to a network or in dis-advantaged environments using peer-to-peer or mesh networks.

Key Features

A native application experience designed for field operations in dynamic and rapidly changing environments. Enabled mission responders with important collaboration capabilities including
  • Work off same designated map, provisioned to the device
  • Multi-mode networking capabilities including P2P and mesh network communication
  • Send status & location updates and see each other’s positions in the field
  • Share information with team members, teams and back to the command center via ArcGIS Mission Manager using:
    • Chat
    • Markup and Points of Interest
    • Documents
    • Photos & Video
  • View Full Motion Video
items.snippet: The mobile application component of ArcGIS Mission, this app equips teams in the field with real-time mobile situational awareness and collaboration capabilities.

items.title: ArcGIS Mission Manager
items.description:
ArcGIS Mission Manager equips teams with mission-focused, real-time situational awareness and collaboration tools for a comprehensive understanding of the operating environment. ArcGIS Mission Manager provides the ability to designate maps and other materials for operations allowing analysts to focus on mission-related tasks such as mission creation, mission monitoring and analysis, and post-mission review and analysis.

Key Features
  1. Pre-mission creation and provisioning to ArcGIS Mission Responder mobile app

    • Select teams
    • Provision designated map
    • Provision supplementary content (forms, documents, etc.)

  2. Active mission monitoring

    • Engage with ArcGIS Mission Responder team members via messages
    • Monitor team member locations tracks
    • Provision and update ArcGIS Mission Responder teams with ad-hoc mission content

  3. Post-mission analysis and playback

    • Capture what happens in the field during a mission including team members tracks, messages, and notes
    • Store captured mission information in ArcGIS Enterprise as a system of record for mission playback further analysis and consumption by the rest of the organization.
items.snippet: The web application component of ArcGIS Mission, this is a focused app for mission managers, analysts and GIS analysts who create, support and manage missions.

items.title: ArcGIS Track Viewer
items.description: Location tracking is an organization-wide capability, providing the ability to record where users are and where they have been. ArcGIS Tracker empowers location tracking, using the location tracking service in two apps: the Track Viewer web app and the ArcGIS Tracker mobile app. The Track Viewer web app allows administrators to create track views, defining which users have tracks included in the view and who can view those tracks. The Tracker mobile app is available on iOS and on Android.
items.snippet: The Track Viewer web app allows administrators to create track views, defining which users have tracks included in the view and who can view those tracks.

items.name: mil2525bc2.stylx
items.title: Joint Military Symbology MIL-STD-2525B Change 2
items.description:
An ArcGIS mobile dictionary style (stylx) file for use with ArcGIS Pro 3.2+ and ArcGIS Maps SDKs for Native Apps 200.2+ to build custom applications that incorporate the MIL-STD-2525B Change 2 symbol dictionary. This style supports a configuration for modeling locations as ordered anchor points or full geometries.

Required Software:
ArcGIS Maps SDKs for Native Apps 200.2 or higher
ArcGIS Pro 3.2 or higher

The style can be published from ArcGIS Pro as a web style for use with the ArcGIS API for JavaScript 4.27 or higher.

Note: Proper drawing of Trip Wire and Counterattack by Fire symbols requires ArcGIS Maps SDKs for Native Apps 200.5 or higher or ArcGIS Pro 3.3 or higher. Proper drawing of Minimum Safe Distance Zone symbols requires ArcGIS Maps SDKs for Native Apps 200.6 or higher, or ArcGIS Pro 3.4 or higher.

items.title: Production Manager for Esri Defense Mapping
items.description:
The Production Manager dashboard provides a modern centralized application for efficiently prioritizing, synchronizing, and managing production jobs across your business units and domains. These production jobs could be the result of customer requests, traditional in-house maintenance, or time-critical operations to support a crisis response effort.

The Production Manager dashboard also provides the ability to comprehensively track, monitor and report on work status. The dashboard uses the job information and metadata in the ArcGIS Workflow Manager database to display reports and status graphs\charts on system operations.

At the management level, the Production Manager dashboard provides Senior Managers and Senior Cartographers with a common view of performance and job tracking functionality. This will include summary metrics and analysis tools to support a common operating picture for planning and decision making.

Key Features
  • Create and manage production jobs in you ArcGIS Workflow Manager database
  • Visualize production status and key metrics of your production jobs in real time
  • Configurable to support any job type from your ArcGIS Workflow Manager database
items.snippet: Prioritize, synchronize, and manage production jobs across your business units and domains.
items.licenseInfo:
Production Manager requires the ArcGIS Workflow Manager for Server extension and a configured ArcGIS Workflow Manager database.

Some features of Production Manager, optionally require the ArcGIS Data Reviewer for Server extension.

Production Manager has been designed to fully support the Esri Defense Mapping Enterprise Production Workflow environment.

items.title: Ortho Maker
items.description:
Ortho Maker allows you to easily upload and process drone imagery. If you are new to drone processing, Ortho Maker’s default settings makes it easy to create accurate products with little to no knowledge of photogrammetric parameters. If you are an advanced drone user, Ortho Maker allows you to fine tune your processing parameters to meet your needs.

Key features:
With Ortho Maker you can:
  • Upload a collection of drone images and process them to create accurate orthoimages, digital elevation models, and analysis products like NDVI.
  • Review your collection of drone images and remove unwanted images.
  • Process your drone imagery with little to no experience in photogrammetry.
  • Upload and manage ground control points to further improve the accuracy of processing results.
  • Fine tune processing parameters if you have experience processing drone images.
  • Review detailed processing reports and share.
  • Share your results for use with other ArcGIS Platform enabled software like Story Maps, ArcGIS Pro, and ArcGIS Image Server’s distributed analytics.

items.title: ArcGIS Insights
items.description:
Part of the Esri Geospatial Cloud, ArcGIS Insights is analysis software that fuses location analytics with open data science and business intelligence workflows. Answer questions you didn’t know to ask, analyze data completely, and unlock new insights.  Empower analyst of all skill levels, across departments, to directly connect data, perform advanced analytics, and take results into 3rd party systems.

 Key Capabilities

  • Perform powerful analysis simply. Explore data and perform advanced analytics such as spatial, statistical, predictive, and link analysis in three clicks or less.
  • Analyze data from multiple sources. Connect to spatial and non-spatial data from spreadsheets, ArcGIS, ArcGIS Living Atlas of the World, and enterprise databases (like SQL Server, SAP HANA, PostgreSQL, and Oracle).
  • Analyze location data without constraints. Accurately map, enrich and analyze location information—an address, city, state, ZIP code, x,y coordinates, place name, or custom boundary.
  • Analyze all your data variables. Use over 20 data visualization styles and a set of spatial analysis capabilities that let you uncover patterns and relationships in your data.
  • Reuse your analysis workflows. Insights automatically saves every step of your analysis and lets you share the data and workflows with others.
  • Leverage Python and R directly within Insights. With these open data science languages, you can integrate machine learning, artificial intelligence, and statistical techniques into your analysis.
  • Share powerful data stories internally and externally. Publish interactive reports that use text, links, images, videos, data visualizations, and your branding.

Need Help?
Visit our documentation page or contact us

items.title: NLCD Demo
items.description:
The National Land Cover Database (NLCD) provides nationwide data on land cover and land cover change at a 30m resolution with a 16-class legend based on a modified Anderson Level II classification system. NLCD 2016 represents the latest evolution of NLCD land cover products focused on providing innovative land cover and land cover change data for the Nation. 

You can find a powerful and flexible version of these data as an ArcGIS Image Service here: https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=3ccf118ed80748909eb85c6d262b426f. And you can read an excellent post about that service here: https://www.esri.com/arcgis-blog/products/arcgis-living-atlas/mapping/mapping-two-decades-of-landcover-change-in-the-u-s/.

The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), in partnership with several federal agencies, has developed and released four National Land Cover Database (NLCD) products over the past two decades: NLCD 1992, 2001, 2006, and 2011. 

These products provide spatially explicit and reliable information on the Nation’s land cover and land cover change. To continue the legacy of NLCD and further establish a long-term monitoring capability for the Nation’s land resources, the USGS has designed a new generation of NLCD products named NLCD 2016. 

The NLCD 2016 design aims to provide innovative, consistent, and robust methodologies for production of a multi-temporal land cover and land cover change database from 2001 to 2016 at 2–3-year intervals. Comprehensive research was conducted and resulted in developed strategies for NLCD 2016: a streamlined process for assembling and preprocessing Landsat imagery and geospatial ancillary datasets; a multi-source integrated training data development and decision-tree based land cover classifications; a temporally, spectrally, and spatially integrated land cover change analysis strategy; a hierarchical theme-based post-classification and integration protocol for generating land cover and change products; a continuous fields biophysical parameters modeling method; and an automated scripted operational system for the NLCD 2016 production. The performance of the developed strategies and methods were tested in twenty World Reference System-2 path/row throughout the conterminous U.S. An overall agreement ranging from 71% to 97% between land cover classification and reference data was achieved for all tested area and all years. 

Results from this study confirm the robustness of this comprehensive and highly automated procedure for NLCD 2016 operational mapping.

A compliant implementation of WMS plus most of the SLD extension (dynamic styling). Can also generate PDF, SVG, KML, GeoRSS

Source: https://www.mrlc.gov/data/nlcd-2016-land-cover-conus
See https://www.mrlc.gov/data for a comprehensive catalog of all available data products.

Find the complete legend here: https://www.mrlc.gov/data/legends/national-land-cover-database-2016-nlcd2016-legend

The Land Use Category field is a generalized Category that follows more closely what Mid-Region Council of Government staff use for their land use modeling activities. items.title: MRMPO Pedestrian Composite Index (PCI)
items.description:
The Pedestrian Composite Index (PCI) is a tool for targeting improvements to pedestrian facilities in places where pedestrian activity is expected to be greatest. Improving walkability and safety in these locations should be prioritized if suitable facilities do not already exist. The National Association of City Transportation Officials (NACTO) recommends wider sidewalks with buffers or planter strips and safer roadway crossings that are closer together.

In the absence of comprehensive sidewalk condition data and pedestrian traffic counts, the PCI projects pedestrian activity on a given street segment based on conditions that potentially generate or attract pedestrian travel.

The Index includes factors such as:
 - proximity to schools, bus stops, parks, and community centers;
 - proximity to higher density areas of jobs and housing;
 - density of roadway connections;
 - transit use; and
 - availability of personal vehicles.

Due to the high pedestrian fatality rates in our region, it is imperative that we work on bringing different methods, data, partners, and approaches together to ensure the pedestrian network and pedestrian safety improve over time.

items.snippet: The CDC\ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) is a tool, created by the Geospatial Research, Analysis and Services Program (GRASP), to help public health officials and emergency response planners identify and map the communities that will most likely need support before, during, and after a hazardous event. The tract-level SVI shows the relative vulnerability of the population of every U.S. Census tract. The county-level SVI shows the relative vulnerability of every U.S. county population. The SVI ranks tracts (or counties) on 16 social factors, described in detail in the documentation. The tract (or county) rankings for individual factors are further grouped into four related themes. Thus each enumeration unit receives a ranking for each Census variable and for each of the four themes, as well as an overall ranking.

items.description: The National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) is a feature-based database that interconnects and uniquely identifies the stream segments or reaches that make up the nation's surface water drainage system. NHD data was originally developed at 1:100,000-scale and exists at that scale for the whole country. This high-resolution NHD, generally developed at 1:24,000/1:12,000 scale, adds detail to the original 1:100,000-scale NHD. (Data for Alaska, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands was developed at high-resolution, not 1:100,000 scale.) Local resolution NHD is being developed where partners and data exist. The NHD contains reach codes for networked features, flow direction, names, and centerline representations for areal water bodies. Reaches are also defined on waterbodies and the approximate shorelines of the Great Lakes, the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and the Gulf of Mexico. The NHD also incorporates the National Spatial Data Infrastructure framework criteria established by the Federal Geographic Data Committee.
items.snippet: The NHD is a national framework for assigning reach addresses to water-related entities, such as industrial discharges, drinking water supplies, fish habitat areas, wild and scenic rivers. Reach addresses establish the locations of these entities relative to one another within the NHD surface water drainage network, much like addresses on streets. Once linked to the NHD by their reach addresses, the upstream/downstream relationships of these water-related entities--and any associated information about them--can be analyzed using software tools ranging from spreadsheets to geographic information systems (GIS). GIS can also be used to combine NHD-based network analysis with other data layers, such as soils, land use and population, to help understand and display their respective effects upon one another. Furthermore, because the NHD provides a nationally consistent framework for addressing and analysis, water-related information linked to reach addresses by one organization (national, state, local) can be shared with other organizations and easily integrated into many different types of applications to the benefit of all.

items.title: HFIN 2017-2021 Story Map
items.description:
The High Fatal & Injury Network (HFIN)  

The HFIN was developed to help target funding to the most dangerous streets and intersections and get the biggest bang for our "safety buck".   

The HFIN symbolizes segments with high levels of fatal and injury crashes per mile, and fatal and injury intersection crash rates (divided by approaching traffic) for every major road (arterials and collectors) in the region.   

The HFIN score is derived from summing the number of fatal and injury crashes on every link and then dividing that number by the length of the link in miles. The number of fatal crashes on each link is multiplied by 2 to give them greater significance than injury crashes.  

The formula for the HFIN Score for any given link is: (fatal crashes *2) + injury crashes/ length of link in miles.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN Score of 319.8 or higher (2 times the regional mean or higher) make up only 2.5% of the major roadway network. However, 26% of the fatalities and 40% of the injury crashes happened on these roadways between 2017 and 2021.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN score of 159.9 or higher (simply above the regional mean) make up only 8% of the major roadways, but contain 47% of the fatal crashes and 64% of the injury crashes. 

Interstates were not included because they are maintained and operated by the NMDOT. For more about NMDOT safety initiatives check out their Planning Division.
items.snippet: A map depicting the most dangerous intersections and segments of roadway in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area.

items.description: The wildland-urban interface (WUI) is the area where houses meet or intermingle with undeveloped wildland vegetation. This makes the WUI a focal area for human-environment conflicts such as wildland fires, habitat fragmentation, invasive species, and biodiversity decline. Using geographic information systems (GIS), we integrated U.S. Census and USGS National Land Cover Data, to map the Federal Register definition of WUI (Federal Register 66:751, 2001) for the conterminous United States from 1990-2010. These data are useful within a GIS for mapping and analysis at national, state, and local levels. Data are available as a geodatabase and include information such as housing and population densities for 1990, 2000, and 2010; wildland vegetation percentages for 1992, 2001, and 2011; as well as WUI classes in 1990, 2000, and 2010.

items.title: CDC Social Vulnerability Index 2020
items.snippet: The CDC\ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) is a tool, created by the Geospatial Research, Analysis and Services Program (GRASP), to help public health officials and emergency response planners identify and map the communities that will most likely need support before, during, and after a hazardous event. The tract-level SVI shows the relative vulnerability of the population of every U.S. Census tract. The county-level SVI shows the relative vulnerability of every U.S. county population. The SVI ranks tracts (or counties) on 16 social factors, described in detail in the documentation. The tract (or county) rankings for individual factors are further grouped into four related themes. Thus each enumeration unit receives a ranking for each Census variable and for each of the four themes, as well as an overall ranking.

items.title: MRCOG_Traffic_Count_Locations
items.description:
This layer is intended for viewing in the MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer app: https://arcg.is/1XXbO51.

MRCOG (Mid-Region Council of Governments; Albuquerque, New Mexico) counts traffic on major roads. Major roads are defined by functional classification and comprise urban minor collectors and above (including rural major collectors and above). The points in this layer represent approximate count locations. They are not intended to represent actual coordinates of past or future counts.

MRCOG collects traffic counts at all major roads in Bernalillo, Valencia, Torrance, Sandoval, and southern Santa Fe counties. The resulting traffic data is used to support local, state, and federal transportation planning activities and to produce annual Traffic Flow Maps for the entire areas within the boundaries of the MRCOG planning area (including both metropolitan and rural areas; https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/623/Traffic-Flow-Maps-and-Busiest-Intersecti).

items.title: LosLunas_MRCOG_Smoothed_Urban_Area_2013
items.description: The Los LunasSmoothed Out Urbanized Area was developed based on input from local municipalities to determine the best way to smooth out the Census-designated Urbanized Area for Los Lunas, New Mexico for transportation planning purposed. The Albuquerque Smoothed Out Urbanized Area was approved by the Metropolitan Transportation Board of the Mid-Region Council of Governments of New Mexico in 2103 through resolution R-13-03. The data is a polygon shapefile that is used to show which areas of the region should be considered urbanized in nature when making decisions about federal aid roadways. However, the location of the line is not detailed enough to be used for determining urban or rural roadways if it coincides with the actual boundary line being placed on a roadway.

items.title: How do crashes impact vulnerable communities? StoryMap
items.description:
Crashes tend to happen at higher rates in communities that have high concentrations of poverty and people of color. Historically, these are the same communities that have been underrepresented in the planning process. Because these neighborhoods bear a disproportionate share of negative societal impacts, they are often referred to as “vulnerable communities”. The Metropolitan Transportation Plan identifies these communities in terms of a regional Environmental Justice (EJ) index.  

See the map below showing fatal crashes with MRCOG's Environmental Justice (EJ) Index. The EJ Index combines the percentage of households living in poverty with the percentage of persons of color in a census tract to create an "EJ score" between 2 and 10. The higher the score, the more vulnerable the community, represented by darker shades in the map below.

items.title: HFIN All Modes Web Map 2017_ 2021
items.description:
The High Fatal & Injury Network (HFIN)  

The HFIN was developed to help target funding to the most dangerous streets and intersections and get the biggest bang for our "safety buck".   

The HFIN symbolizes segments with high levels of fatal and injury crashes per mile, and fatal and injury intersection crash rates (divided by approaching traffic) for every major road (arterials and collectors) in the region.   

The HFIN score is derived from summing the number of fatal and injury crashes on every link and then dividing that number by the length of the link in miles. The number of fatal crashes on each link is multiplied by 2 to give them greater significance than injury crashes.  

The formula for the HFIN Score for any given link is: (fatal crashes *2) + injury crashes/ length of link in miles.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN Score of 319.8 or higher (2 times the regional mean or higher) make up only 2.5% of the major roadway network. However, 26% of the fatalities and 40% of the injury crashes happened on these roadways between 2017 and 2021.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN score of 159.9 or higher (simply above the regional mean) make up only 8% of the major roadways, but contain 47% of the fatal crashes and 64% of the injury crashes. 

Interstates were not included because they are maintained and operated by the NMDOT. For more about NMDOT safety initiatives check out their Planning Division.

items.name: Household_Poverty___Bernalillo_County___2014_and_2019
items.title: Household Poverty _ Bernalillo County _ 2014 and 2019
items.description:
MRMPO shares these layers solely for the purpose of visualizing basic poverty information based on US Census Bureau geographies and statistics.

Tract boundaries are from 2019 Tiger state geodatabase for New Mexico (35), selected for Bernalillo County (001).
Poverty data (2015-2019) is from American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year data, table B17017, 2019.
Poverty data (2010-2014) is from American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year data, table B17017, 2014.
Each layer has an added field (HHPovPerc) with a calculated percentage of households per tract with income below the national poverty level. The calculation used was as follows: 100 * B17017_002E / B17017_001E, or 100 times the quotient of estimated households with income below poverty level divided by estimated total households. Calculations were done per tract. Field names are defined in the "Table Shells" data dictionaries linked below.

Additional information:
Tiger geodatabases: https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/tiger-geodatabase-file.html
American community survey and other Census data: https://data.census.gov/cedsci/ 
2019 Table shells: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/technical-documentation/table-shells.2019.html
2014 Table shells: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/technical-documentation/table-shells.2014.html
items.snippet: Census tracts (2019) for Bernalillo County joined to ACS table B17017 (poverty by household). One sublayer uses 2014 5-year data (2010-2014) and one sublayer uses 2019 5-year data (2015-2019).

items.title: AMPA Historically Disadvantaged Communities
items.description:
"The Biden-Harris Administration created the Justice40 Initiative to confront and address decades of underinvestment in disadvantaged communities. The initiative will bring resources to communities most impacted by climate change, pollution, and environmental hazards."

In February 2022 the White House Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) released The Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool (CEJST in beta form.  The tool aims to help Federal agencies identify disadvantaged communities (DACs) that are marginalized, underserved, and overburdened by pollution as part of the Justice40 Initiative.  While CEJST is still in beta, the Department is using an interim definition to identify disadvantaged communities for Justice40-covered programs, consistent with Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance and relevant statutory authorities. DOT is using this interim definition to ask applicants to Justice40-covered programs to identify how their projects benefit DACs.

USDOT’s interim definition of DACs includes (a) certain qualifying census tracts, (b) any Tribal land, or (c) any territory or possession of the United States. USDOT has provided a mapping tool to assist applicants in identifying whether a project is located in a Disadvantaged Community, available at Transportation Disadvantaged Census Tracts.  

A shapefile of the geospatial data is available, and this map is made from an export from that shapefile to identify DACs within the Albuquerque Metro Planning Area.  To learn more about Justice40 covered funding opportunities and the USDOT's implementation efforts, see: https://www.transportation.gov/equity-Justice40

items.title: MRCOG Vulnerability Indices 2016-2020
items.description:
Based on the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) of the Center for Disease Control and Prevention, the MRMPO Vulnerability Index (MVI) score provides an indicator of the relative ability of communities to survive and thrive when confronted by external stresses on human health, such as exposure to environmental pollution and the hazards associated with climate change. In additional to the demographic factors included in the SVI methodology,* the MVI adds measures of gender, ethnic and national origin. 

Using 2016-2020 census American Community Survey (ACS) data, tract-level demographic information is provided in a pop-up window by clicking on the map, and percent ranked (percentile) variables are combined into one percentile value representing a comparative measure of resident population vulnerability relative to other tracts in the regional or metropolitan area.

An additional score is provided as an indication of the residential concentration of those populations of special concern for environmental justice considerations - "low-income and minority" populations, or persons of color, of Hispanic/Latine ethnicity, and those with annual incomes below the federal poverty level.

*Demographic indicators of social vulnerability:

  • Socioeconomic Status
    • Below 150% Poverty
    • Unemployed
    • Housing Cost Burden
    • No High School Diploma
    • No Health Insurance
  • Household Characteristics
    • Aged 65 & Older
    • Aged 17 & Younger
    • Civilian with a Disability
    • Single-Parent Households
    • English Language Proficiency
  • Racial & Ethnic Minority Status
    • Hispanic or Latino (of any race); Black and African American; American Indian and Alaska Native; Asian; Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander; Two or More Races; Other Races
  • Housing Type & Transportation
    • Multi-Unit Structures
    • Mobile Homes
    • Crowding
    • No Vehicle
    • Group Quarters
items.snippet: Map visualizing social vulnerability indices of the Albuquerque Metro and Regional Planning Areas, shaded to represent the relative concentration of populations of concern for equity and protection from harm. Among other contributing factors*, vulnerable populations include children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities.

items.title: MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer
items.description:
MRCOG collects traffic counts at all major roads in Bernalillo, Valencia, Torrance, Sandoval, and southern Santa Fe counties. The resulting traffic data is used to support local, state, and federal transportation planning activities and to produce annual Traffic Flow Maps for the entire areas within the boundaries of the MRCOG planning area (including both metropolitan and rural areas; https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/623/Traffic-Flow-Maps-and-Busiest-Intersecti). 

Most traffic counts are performed using portable traffic monitoring devices with rubber tubes that stretch across the roadway (pneumonic tube counters). 

Additional traffic data is collected by the New Mexico Department of Transportation through a series of permanent count stations on Interstates and certain arterials. These locations provide continuous data-reporting which is also used for seasonal factoring for annualized data averaging from the short-term counts as noted above. 

All major roads functionally-classified as collectors or higher are counted on a periodic schedule every three years. Traffic monitoring devices are placed at a location for 48 hours to produce average daily and peak period traffic volume levels, as well as directional split values (the percentage of travel in each direction for the day or peak period). Devices are set out on Mondays or Tuesdays and picked up on Wednesdays or Thursdays. Growth factors are applied in the intervening years and seasonal factors are applied based on the time of year the count was taken to generate yearly data.

For more information, please visit our website: https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/285/Traffic-Monitoring.

Problems viewing the app? Please contact gis@mrcog-nm.gov.
items.snippet: A web app for viewing traffic counts in the MRCOG region. Counts are presented by roadway section and by approximate count locations. Features include tabular data exports and basic map exports.
items.licenseInfo:
This app, and all maps and data contained within, are intended for general reference purposes only.

Additional statistical information is available upon request. MRMPO occasionally collects traffic data for special studies, requested by our member agencies. Additionally, there are summary reports that include vehicle classification, Vehicle Hours Traveled (VHT) and Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) for the region. For more information, please visit our website: https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/285/Traffic-Monitoring.

items.title: Tribal_Areas_BIA_LAR_MRCOG
items.description:
The purpose of the American Indian and Alaska Native Land Area Representation (AIAN-LAR) Geographic Information System (GIS) dataset is to depict the external extent of federal Indian reservations and the external extent of associated land held in “trust” by the United States, “restricted fee” or “mixed ownership” status for federally recognized tribes and individual Indians. This dataset includes other land area types such as Public Domain Allotments, Dependent Indian Communities and Homesteads.

This GIS Dataset is prepared strictly for illustrative and reference purposes only and should not be used, and is not intended for legal, survey, engineering or navigation purposes.

No warranty is made by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) for the use of the data for purposes not intended by the BIA. This GIS Dataset may contain errors. There is no impact on the legal status of the land areas depicted herein and no impact on land ownership. No legal inference can or should be made from the information in this GIS Dataset. The GIS Dataset is to be used solely for illustrative, reference and statistical purposes and may be used for government to government Tribal consultation.

Reservation boundary data is limited in authority to those areas where there has been settled Congressional definition or final judicial interpretation of the boundary. Absent settled Congressional definition or final judicial interpretation of a reservation boundary, the BIA recommends consultation with the appropriate Tribe and then the BIA to obtain interpretations of the reservation boundary.

The land areas and their representations are compilations defined by the official land title records of the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) which include treaties, statutes, Acts of Congress, agreements, executive orders, proclamations, deeds and other land title documents. The trust, restricted, and mixed ownership land area shown here, are suitable only for general spatial reference and do not represent the federal government’s position on the jurisdictional status of Indian country. Ownership and jurisdictional status is subject to change and must be verified with plat books, patents, and deeds in the appropriate federal and state offices.

Included in this dataset are the exterior extent of off reservation trust, restricted fee tracts and mixed tracts of land including Public Domain allotments, Dependent Indian Communities, Homesteads and government administered lands and those set aside for schools and dormitories. There are also land areas where there is more than one tribe having an interest in or authority over a tract of land but this information is not specified in the AIAN-LAR dataset. The dataset includes both surface and subsurface tracts of land (tribal and individually held) “off reservation” tracts and not simply off reservation “allotments” as land has in many cases been subsequently acquired in trust.

These data are public information and may be used by various organizations, agencies, units of government (i.e., Federal, state, county, and city), and other entities according to the restrictions on appropriate use. It is strongly recommended that these data be acquired directly from the BIA and not indirectly through some other source, which may have altered or integrated the data for another purpose for which they may not have been intended. Integrating land areas into another dataset and attempting to resolve boundary differences between other entities may produce inaccurate results. It is also strongly recommended that careful attention be paid to the content of the metadata file associated with these data. Users are cautioned that digital enlargement of these data to scales greater than those at which they were originally mapped can cause misinterpretation.

The BIA AIAN-LAR dataset’s spatial accuracy and attribute information are continuously being updated, improved and is used as the single authoritative land area boundary data for the BIA mission. These data are available through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, Office of Trust Services, Division of Land Titles and Records, Branch of Geospatial Support.

items.title: HFIN Bicyclists Web Map 2017_2021
items.description:
The High Fatal & Injury Network (HFIN)  

The HFIN was developed to help target funding to the most dangerous streets and intersections and get the biggest bang for our "safety buck".   

The HFIN symbolizes segments with high levels of fatal and injury crashes per mile, and fatal and injury intersection crash rates (divided by approaching traffic) for every major road (arterials and collectors) in the region.   

The HFIN score is derived from summing the number of fatal and injury crashes on every link and then dividing that number by the length of the link in miles. The number of fatal crashes on each link is multiplied by 2 to give them greater significance than injury crashes.  

The formula for the HFIN Score for any given link is: (fatal crashes *2) + injury crashes/ length of link in miles.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN Score of 319.8 or higher (2 times the regional mean or higher) make up only 2.5% of the major roadway network. However, 26% of the fatalities and 40% of the injury crashes happened on these roadways between 2017 and 2021.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN score of 159.9 or higher (simply above the regional mean) make up only 8% of the major roadways, but contain 47% of the fatal crashes and 64% of the injury crashes. 

Interstates were not included because they are maintained and operated by the NMDOT. For more about NMDOT safety initiatives check out their Planning Division.

items.title: MRMPO Regional Data Viewer v1.0
items.description:
An interactive web mapping application featuring a variety of transportation planning datasets maintained by the Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO) in Albuquerque, NM, USA. 

The layers in this map are consistent with the goals of Connections 2040 long-range Metropolitan Transportation Plan (MTP). They include transportation data such as roadway congestion, bike facilities, and crash data, as well as land use data such as major Activity Centers. Data shown in this viewer may be incorporated into the ongoing update of the Project Prioritization Process (PPP) that will support the 2024 - 2029 Transportation Improvement Plan (TIP). The 2024 - 2029 TIP begins development in the fall of 2022.

Please note that in the development of the MTP, 2016 was considered the base year (2012 for activity density) and data for base years are estimates, while data for the 2040 horizon year are projections.

https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/233/Metropolitan-Planning-Organization

Version 1.0 was published in October 2021.

items.title: HFIN Pedestrians Web Map 2017 _2021
items.description:
The High Fatal & Injury Network (HFIN)  

The HFIN was developed to help target funding to the most dangerous streets and intersections and get the biggest bang for our "safety buck".   

The HFIN symbolizes segments with high levels of fatal and injury crashes per mile, and fatal and injury intersection crash rates (divided by approaching traffic) for every major road (arterials and collectors) in the region.   

The HFIN score is derived from summing the number of fatal and injury crashes on every link and then dividing that number by the length of the link in miles. The number of fatal crashes on each link is multiplied by 2 to give them greater significance than injury crashes.  

The formula for the HFIN Score for any given link is: (fatal crashes *2) + injury crashes/ length of link in miles.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN Score of 319.8 or higher (2 times the regional mean or higher) make up only 2.5% of the major roadway network. However, 26% of the fatalities and 40% of the injury crashes happened on these roadways between 2017 and 2021.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN score of 159.9 or higher (simply above the regional mean) make up only 8% of the major roadways, but contain 47% of the fatal crashes and 64% of the injury crashes. 

Interstates were not included because they are maintained and operated by the NMDOT. For more about NMDOT safety initiatives check out their Planning Division.

items.title: Disadvantaged Census Tracts of USDOT Screening Tool
items.description:
"The Biden-Harris Administration created the Justice40 Initiative to confront and address decades of underinvestment in disadvantaged communities. The initiative will bring resources to communities most impacted by climate change, pollution, and environmental hazards."

In February 2022 the White House Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) released The Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool (CEJST in beta form.  The tool aims to help Federal agencies identify disadvantaged communities (DACs) that are marginalized, underserved, and overburdened by pollution as part of the Justice40 Initiative.  While CEJST is still in beta, the Department is using an interim definition to identify disadvantaged communities for Justice40-covered programs, consistent with Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance and relevant statutory authorities. DOT is using this interim definition to ask applicants to Justice40-covered programs to identify how their projects benefit DACs.

Consistent with OMB’s Interim Guidance for the Justice40 Initiative, DOT’s interim definition of DACs includes (a) certain qualifying census tracts, (b) any Tribal land, or (c) any territory or possession of the United States. DOT has provided a mapping tool to assist applicants in identifying whether a project is located in a Disadvantaged Community, available at Transportation Disadvantaged Census Tracts (https://usdot.maps.arcgis.com/apps/dashboards/d6f90dfcc8b44525b04c7ce748a3674a).  

A shapefile of the geospatial data is available, and this layer is an export from the shapefile for tracts within the Albuquerque Metro Planning Area.  To learn more about Justice40 covered funding opportunities and the USDOT's implementation efforts, see: https://www.transportation.gov/equity-Justice40

items.title: MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer Map
items.description:
This map is intended for viewing in the MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer app: https://arcg.is/1XXbO51.

MRCOG collects traffic counts at all major roads in Bernalillo, Valencia, Torrance, Sandoval, and southern Santa Fe counties. The resulting traffic data is used to support local, state, and federal transportation planning activities and to produce annual Traffic Flow Maps for the entire areas within the boundaries of the MRCOG planning area (including both metropolitan and rural areas; https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/623/Traffic-Flow-Maps-and-Busiest-Intersecti). 

Most traffic counts are performed using portable traffic monitoring devices with rubber tubes that stretch across the roadway (pneumonic tube counters). 

Additional traffic data is collected by the New Mexico Department of Transportation through a series of permanent count stations on Interstates and certain arterials. These locations provide continuous data-reporting which is also used for seasonal factoring for annualized data averaging from the short-term counts as noted above. 

All major roads functionally-classified as collectors or higher are counted on a periodic schedule every three years. Traffic monitoring devices are placed at a location for 48 hours to produce average daily and peak period traffic volume levels, as well as directional split values (the percentage of travel in each direction for the day or peak period). Devices are set out on Mondays or Tuesdays and picked up on Wednesdays or Thursdays. Growth factors are applied in the intervening years and seasonal factors are applied based on the time of year the count was taken to generate yearly data.

For more information, please visit our website: https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/285/Traffic-Monitoring.

Problems viewing the app? Please contact gis@mrcog-nm.gov.

items.snippet: CDC's Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) is a tool, created by the Geospatial Research, Analysis & Services Program (GRASP), to help public health officials and emergency response planners identify and map the communities that will most likely need support before, during, and after a hazardous event. The tract-level SVI shows the relative vulnerability of the population of every U.S. Census tract. The county-level SVI shows the relative vulnerability of every U.S. county population. The SVI ranks tracts (or counties) on 15 social factors, described in detail in the documentation. The tract (or county) rankings for individual factors are further grouped into four related themes. Thus each enumeration unit receives a ranking for each Census variable and for each of the four themes, as well as an overall ranking.

items.title: MRCOG Vulnerability Indices 2016-2020
items.description:
Based on the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) of the Center for DiseaseControl and Prevention, the MRMPO Vulnerability Index (MVI) score provides an indicator of the relative ability of communities to survive and thrive when confronted by external stresses on human health, such as exposure to environmental pollution and the hazards associated with climate change. In addition to the demographic factors included in the SVI methodology,* the MVI adds measures of gender, ethnic and national origin. 

Using 2016-2020 census American Community Survey (ACS) data, tract-level demographic information is provided in a pop-up window by clicking on the map, and percent ranked (percentile) variables are combined into one percentile value representing a comparative measure of resident population vulnerability relative to other tracts in the regional or metropolitan area.

An additional score is provided as an indication of the residential concentration of those populations of special concern for environmental justice considerations - "low-income and minority" populations, or persons of color, of Hispanic/Latine ethnicity, and those with annual incomes below the federal poverty level.

*Demographic indicators of social vulnerability:

  • Socioeconomic Status
    • Below 150% Poverty
    • Unemployed
    • Housing Cost Burden
    • No High School Diploma
    • No Health Insurance
  • Household Characteristics
    • Aged 65 & Older
    • Aged 17 & Younger
    • Civilian with a Disability
    • Single-Parent Households
    • English Language Proficiency
  • Racial & Ethnic Minority Status
    • Hispanic or Latino (of any race); Black and African American; American Indian and Alaska Native; Asian; Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander; Two or More Races; Other Races
  • Housing Type & Transportation
    • Multi-Unit Structures
    • Mobile Homes
    • Crowding
    • No Vehicle
    • Group Quarters

items.description: This map includes data from 2011 to 2015 in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area. The data in this map is specifically fatal and injury crashes. The map depicts roadway segments where the crashes per mile are above the mean. The HFIN includes only those that are 2x above the mean. Some acronyms are used including LU = Large Urban area, SU = Small Urban area, and RU = Rural area. This map was created by the Mid Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO). These are created based on federal funding categories. Please contact Caeri Thomas at cthomas@mrcog-nm.gov with any questions.

items.licenseInfo:
•This is a sample of the data – it may not contain all crashes that have happened.
•There are also crashes that are never reported.
•The crash data is provided by University of New Mexico Geospatial Population Studies department, whose staff geocode the crash record data. Complete accuracy of geographic coordinate is not guaranteed.
•The data is acquired and reviewed by the New Mexico Department of Transportation’s (NMDOT) Traffic Safety Bureau from police records across the State of New Mexico.
•A crash must involve at least one motor vehicle, occur on a public roadway, and result in at least $500 of property damage or personal injury.
•This crash data, along with Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization’s major roads street network and traffic counts data, allow for calculating crash rates for the region.
•Fatality and injury crashes are the focus of this plan because these crashes are associated with the greatest human and financial cost to the public.

items.title: MRCOG_Traffic_Count_Segments
items.description:
This layer is intended for viewing in the MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer app: https://arcg.is/1XXbO51.

MRCOG (Mid-Region Council of Governments; Albuquerque, New Mexico) counts traffic on major roads. Major roads are defined by functional classification and comprise urban minor collectors and above (including rural major collectors and above). Traffic counts are shown by road segment (also called edges or links) - a contiguous section of road from one major intersection to the next. Counts are calculated for both annual average daily traffic (ADT) and annual average weekday traffic (AWDT).

MRCOG collects traffic counts at all major roads in Bernalillo, Valencia, Torrance, Sandoval, and southern Santa Fe counties. The resulting traffic data is used to support local, state, and federal transportation planning activities and to produce annual Traffic Flow Maps for the entire areas within the boundaries of the MRCOG planning area (including both metropolitan and rural areas; https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/623/Traffic-Flow-Maps-and-Busiest-Intersecti).

Additional statistical information is available upon request. MRMPO occasionally collects traffic data for special studies, requested by our member agencies. Additionally, there are summary reports that include vehicle classification, Vehicle Hours Traveled (VHT) and Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) for the region. For more information, please visit our website: https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/285/Traffic-Monitoring.

The layers in this map are consistent with the goals of Connections 2040 long-range Metropolitan Transportation Plan (MTP). They include transportation data such as roadway congestion, bike facilities, and crash data, as well as land use data such as major Activity Centers. Data shown in this viewer may be incorporated into the ongoing update of the Project Prioritization Process (PPP) that will support the 2024 - 2029 Transportation Improvement Plan (TIP). The 2024 - 2029 TIP begins development in the fall of 2022.

Please note that in the development of the MTP, 2016 was considered the base year (2012 for activity density) and data for base years are estimates, while data for the 2040 horizon year are projections.

items.title: MRMPO Pedestrian Composite Index (PCI) App
items.description:
The Pedestrian Composite Index (PCI) is a tool for targeting improvements to pedestrian facilities in places where pedestrian activity is expected to be greatest. Improving walkability and safety in these locations should be prioritized if suitable facilities do not already exist. The National Association of City Transportation Officials (NACTO) recommends wider sidewalks with buffers or planter strips and safer roadway crossings that are closer together.

In the absence of comprehensive sidewalk condition data and pedestrian traffic counts, the PCI projects pedestrian activity on a given street segment based on conditions that potentially generate or attract pedestrian travel.

The Index includes factors such as:
 - proximity to schools, bus stops, parks, and community centers;
 - proximity to higher density areas of jobs and housing;
 - density of roadway connections;
 - transit use; and
 - availability of personal vehicles.

Due to the high pedestrian fatality rates in our region, it is imperative that we work on bringing different methods, data, partners, and approaches together to ensure the pedestrian network and pedestrian safety improve over time.

items.description:
The Long Range Transit Network (LRTN) describes an aspirational transit network that envisions new transit services - including a new bus rapid transit (BRT) route and several new rapid ride routes - along with the region's existing bus and commuter rail services.

As with other Long Range Systems, the LRTN is designed to support the principles of the 2040 Target Scenario. In particular, the network seeks to connect activity centers and support future mixed-use corridors. Expanded transit would also provide increased options for crossing the river.

items.title: Road Diets in the Albuquerque Region
items.description: This map includes data from 2011 to 2015 in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area. The data in this map is specifically fatal and injury crashes. The map depicts roadway segments where the crashes per mile are above the mean. The HFIN includes only those that are 2x above the mean. Some acronyms are used including LU = Large Urban area, SU = Small Urban area, and RU = Rural area. This map was created by the Mid Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO). These are created based on federal funding categories. Please contact Caeri Thomas at cthomas@mrcog-nm.gov with any questions.
items.snippet: Shows the high fatal and injury network plus potential road diet candidates based on traffic volume and number of lanes.
items.licenseInfo:
•This is a sample of the data – it may not contain all crashes that have happened.
•There are also crashes that are never reported.
•The crash data is provided by University of New Mexico Geospatial Population Studies department, whose staff geocode the crash record data. Complete accuracy of geographic coordinate is not guaranteed.
•The data is acquired and reviewed by the New Mexico Department of Transportation’s (NMDOT) Traffic Safety Bureau from police records across the State of New Mexico.
•A crash must involve at least one motor vehicle, occur on a public roadway, and result in at least $500 of property damage or personal injury.
•This crash data, along with Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization’s major roads street network and traffic counts data, allow for calculating crash rates for the region.
•Fatality and injury crashes are the focus of this plan because these crashes are associated with the greatest human and financial cost to the public.

items.description: The boundary of the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area (AMPA) was adopted in 2012 by the Metropolitan Transportation Board of the Mid-Region Council of Governments of New Mexico through resolution R-12-13 MTB. The 2012 boundary expanded the AMPA to include all of Valencia County, Bernalillo County, and the southeastern portion of Sandoval County. Metropolitan Planning Organizations (MPOs) are required by federal law for all urbanized areas with populations greater than 50,000. MPO's are responsible for carrying out metropolitan transportation plans and programs. The MPO for the AMPA is the Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization. The Metropolitan Transportation Board, composed of local elected leaders, sets policy for transportation issues in the urban area.

items.title: CABQ_LandUse_RSAarea
items.description: Land use for areas within the City of Albuquerque. The land use codes were converted to a new set of codes in March 2019 in coordination between the City of Albuquerque Planning Department Urban Design and Development and AGIS Divisions and staff at Mid-Region Council of Governments. The Land Use Category field is a generalized Category that follows more closely what Mid-Region Council of Government staff use for their land use modeling activities. The Land Use Description field follows more closely the types of land uses outlined in the Integrated Development Ordinance (IDO) that became effective May 17, 2018. These Use Regulations are listed in Part 14-16-4 within the document. The Old Land Use Category field is how the Land Use layer was generalized prior to March 2019 (starting from the mid-1990s) and the Old Land Use Description field includes the codes that were in use prior to March 2019 (starting from the mid-1990s). These codes will remain in place until it is determined by AGIS that they are no longer needed. Updates to the land uses are ongoing, including an effort starting March 2019 from direct feedback supplied by Urban Design and Development staff.

items.description: The Albuquerque Smoothed Out Urbanized Area was developed based on input from local municipalities to determine the best way to smooth out the Census-designated Urbanized Area for Albuquerque, New Mexico for transportation planning purposed. The Albuquerque Smoothed Out Urbanized Area was approved by the Metropolitan Transportation Board of the Mid-Region Council of Governments of New Mexico in 2013 through resolution R-13-03. The data is a polygon shapefile that is used to show which areas of the region should be considered urbanized in nature when making decisions about federal aid roadways. However, the location of the line is not detailed enough to be used for determining urban or rural roadways if it coincides with the actual boundary line being placed on a roadway.

This dynamic web map offers a seamless and intuitive interface for users to explore, analyze, and access geospatial data relevant to bridge planning and management.

The Bridge Locator Web Map serves as an indispensable tool for in-house teams engaged in bridge planning, maintenance, and decision-making. By providing real-time access to accurate bridge data, this map enhances operational efficiency and promotes informed choices. Its streamlined approach to displaying vital bridge information ensures that users can swiftly identify relevant details, ultimately contributing to efficient bridge management and informed decision-making processes.

items.title: MRMPO Pedestrian Composite Index (PCI)
items.description:
The Pedestrian Composite Index (PCI) is a tool for targeting improvements to pedestrian facilities in places where pedestrian activity is expected to be greatest. Improving walkability and safety in these locations should be prioritized if suitable facilities do not already exist. The National Association of City Transportation Officials (NACTO) recommends wider sidewalks with buffers or planter strips and safer roadway crossings that are closer together.

In the absence of comprehensive sidewalk condition data and pedestrian traffic counts, the PCI projects pedestrian activity on a given street segment based on conditions that potentially generate or attract pedestrian travel.

The Index includes factors such as:
 - proximity to schools, bus stops, parks, and community centers;
 - proximity to higher density areas of jobs and housing;
 - density of roadway connections;
 - transit use; and
 - availability of personal vehicles.

Due to the high pedestrian fatality rates in our region, it is imperative that we work on bringing different methods, data, partners, and approaches together to ensure the pedestrian network and pedestrian safety improve over time.

items.title: Roadway Bicycle Guidelines
items.description:
Welcome to NMDOT's
Roadway Bicycle Guideline
Map

The New Mexico Department of Transportation's State Bicycle Guideline Map is provided to assist cyclists in choosing preferred routes when bicycling through New Mexico. The map shows usable shoulder width estimates, presence of rumble strips, and segments of steep grade for all NMDOT-owned roads in New Mexico. The map also includes a more detailed layer of bicycle facilities in the Albuquerque area, provided by the Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO).

Usable shoulder width estimates were adjusted shoulder data depending on the presence of rumble strips, guardrails or other adjacent barriers. Traffic volumes are derived from averages, and you may experience more or less traffic than displayed on the map. When bicycling throughout New Mexico, please make sure to plan accordingly. Call ahead to communities and potential service providers to verify that your destination has the services you need or want. Some areas of the state are quite remote and uninhabited. While these are some of the very qualities that draw visitors to New Mexico, please note that some communities displayed on our map may not have the services you expect. Further, all information contained on this map is subject to change. We hope you enjoy your bicycling trips throughout the Land of Enchantment! Whether you are climbing mountain passes or enjoying the long open road, our wonderful climate, incomparable vistas, and unique history are sure to provide you with a memorable experience.

In case of Emergency, call 911. New Mexico Roads provides information on current roadway conditions, including construction. Please call 511 or visit NMRoads.com for more information. Please read the Notice of Disclaimer under Access and Use Constraints.

This map includes a layer with bicycle facility data from the Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO) showing bikeway facilities in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area (AMPA) which includes Bernalillo County, Valencia County, and part of Sandoval County.

MRMPO defines their bicycle facility data terms as follows:
•    BIKE LANE = division of roadway marked off with painted lines for use by bicyclists.
•    BIKE ROUTE = a roadway with appropriate direction and informational signing for bicyclists, usually on low-speed, low-traffic streets.
•    BIKE BOULEVARD = a bike route that is designed to prioritize bicycle through movement while also maintaining local access for motor vehicles. Often bicycle boulevards include a variety of traffic calming measures. They are also known as Neighborhood Greenways.
•    MULTI-USE TRAIL = a pathway that is physically separated from the roadway for pedestrians, bicyclists, and wheelchair users.

Most trails are designed for two-way traffic. For questions related to MRMPO data specifically, please contact Tara Cok at the Mid-Region Council of Governments (MRCOG). MRCOG phone number: (505) 247-1750.

For bicycle maps and resources from various communities in New Mexico, please follow the links below:

•    Albuquerque region bike map
•    Farmington city bike map
•    Santa Fe region bike map

The unpredictable change of traffic, road, and weather conditions require bicyclists to consistently review all routes for suitability. Therefore, bicyclists assume all risks and responsibilities for their own safety when bicycling on the roadways and bikeways within the State.

Moreover, bicyclists should be familiar with State and local laws and ordinances concerning bicycle use on roadways and bikeways. items.snippet: The CDC\ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) is a tool, created by the Geospatial Research, Analysis and Services Program (GRASP), to help public health officials and emergency response planners identify and map the communities that will most likely need support before, during, and after a hazardous event. The tract-level SVI shows the relative vulnerability of the population of every U.S. Census tract. The county-level SVI shows the relative vulnerability of every U.S. county population. The SVI ranks tracts (or counties) on 16 social factors, described in detail in the documentation. The tract (or county) rankings for individual factors are further grouped into four related themes. Thus each enumeration unit receives a ranking for each Census variable and for each of the four themes, as well as an overall ranking.

items.title: Long Range Roadway System 2040
items.description:
The Long Range Roadway System (LRRS) provides future recommended roadways and their regional role. This system should be viewed as an aspiration network. That is, the map demonstrates how the region's roadways are envisioned to function as a network with some roads closer to their desired functionality than others. This system also identify future basic network connectivity needs. 

The Long Range Roadway System does not provide current functional classification that determines if the roadway is eligible for federal funds. Instead, the LRRS, builds upon the functional classification categories by considering the character of the roadway and the role it plays in the regional network. The main distinction is differentiating principle arterials into two groups: regional and community. Regional principle arterials are primarily for travel across the region with high levels of access management, whereas trips on community principle arterials are shorter and tend to be be to destinations with direct access off the arterial.  

Future roadways that are beyond the 2040 time frame are highlighted in grey. 

This map is created and updated by the Mid-Region Council of Governments Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO). It is updated concurrently with the Metropolitan Transportation Plan (MTP).

items.title: MRMPO_Cities
items.description:
The TIGER/Line shapefiles and related database files (.dbf) are an extract of selected geographic and cartographic information from the U.S. Census Bureau's Master Address File / Topologically Integrated Geographic Encoding and Referencing (MAF/TIGER) Database (MTDB). The MTDB represents a seamless national file with no overlaps or gaps between parts, however, each TIGER/Line shapefile is designed to stand alone as an independent data set, or they can be combined to cover the entire nation.

The TIGER/Line shapefiles include both incorporated places (legal entities) and census designated places or CDPs (statistical entities). An incorporated place is established to provide governmental functions for a concentration of people as opposed to a minor civil division (MCD), which generally is created to provide services or administer an area without regard, necessarily, to population. Places always nest within a state, but may extend across county and county subdivision boundaries. An incorporated place usually is a city, town, village, or borough, but can have other legal descriptions. CDPs are delineated for the decennial census as the statistical counterparts of incorporated places. CDPs are delineated to provide data for settled concentrations of population that are identifiable by name, but are not legally incorporated under the laws of the state in which they are located. The boundaries for CDPs often are defined in partnership with state, local, and/or tribal officials and usually coincide with visible features or the boundary of an adjacent incorporated place or another legal entity. CDP boundaries often change from one decennial census to the next with changes in the settlement pattern and development; a CDP with the same name as in an earlier census does not necessarily have the same boundary. The only population/housing size requirement for CDPs is that they must contain some housing and population.

The boundaries of most incorporated places in this shapefile are as of January 1, 2017, as reported through the Census Bureau's Boundary and Annexation Survey (BAS). The boundaries of all CDPs were delineated as part of the Census Bureau's Participant Statistical Areas Program (PSAP) for the 2010 Census.
tags: Governmental Units and Administrative and Statistical Boundaries Theme
items.snippet: In order for others to use the information in the Census MAF/TIGER database in a geographic information system (GIS) or for other geographic applications, the Census Bureau releases to the public extracts of the database in the form of TIGER/Line Shapefiles.

items.title: Bridge / MilePost LookUp App
items.description:
The in-house "Bridge / MilePost Web App" is a user-friendly and efficient solution designed to showcase the locations of bridges, mileposts, and hundredths along roadways. With its intuitive interface, this web app enables users to easily visualize and navigate through bridge locations while accessing accurate milepost and hundredth information.

Users can input specific milepost and hundredth values to pinpoint precise bridge locations or explore the app's interactive map to identify bridges within a chosen area. The app provides a comprehensive overview of the entire bridge network, making it a valuable tool for internal teams tasked with maintenance, inspection, and planning.

With its specialized focus on bridges, mileposts, and hundredths, the web app optimizes data access and presentation, enhancing operational efficiency. By streamlining the process of locating and assessing bridges, this in-house solution significantly contributes to informed decision-making and effective management of roadway infrastructure.

items.title: CDC Social Vulnerability Index 2020
items.snippet: The CDC\ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) is a tool, created by the Geospatial Research, Analysis and Services Program (GRASP), to help public health officials and emergency response planners identify and map the communities that will most likely need support before, during, and after a hazardous event. The tract-level SVI shows the relative vulnerability of the population of every U.S. Census tract. The county-level SVI shows the relative vulnerability of every U.S. county population. The SVI ranks tracts (or counties) on 16 social factors, described in detail in the documentation. The tract (or county) rankings for individual factors are further grouped into four related themes. Thus each enumeration unit receives a ranking for each Census variable and for each of the four themes, as well as an overall ranking.

items.title: MRCOG_Traffic_Count_Locations
items.description:
This layer is intended for viewing in the MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer app: https://arcg.is/1XXbO51.

MRCOG (Mid-Region Council of Governments; Albuquerque, New Mexico) counts traffic on major roads. Major roads are defined by functional classification and comprise urban minor collectors and above (including rural major collectors and above). The points in this layer represent approximate count locations. They are not intended to represent actual coordinates of past or future counts.

MRCOG collects traffic counts at all major roads in Bernalillo, Valencia, Torrance, Sandoval, and southern Santa Fe counties. The resulting traffic data is used to support local, state, and federal transportation planning activities and to produce annual Traffic Flow Maps for the entire areas within the boundaries of the MRCOG planning area (including both metropolitan and rural areas; https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/623/Traffic-Flow-Maps-and-Busiest-Intersecti).

Additional statistical information is available upon request. MRMPO occasionally collects traffic data for special studies, requested by our member agencies.
