items.description: The Los LunasSmoothed Out Urbanized Area was developed based on input from local municipalities to determine the best way to smooth out the Census-designated Urbanized Area for Los Lunas, New Mexico for transportation planning purposed. The Albuquerque Smoothed Out Urbanized Area was approved by the Metropolitan Transportation Board of the Mid-Region Council of Governments of New Mexico in 2103 through resolution R-13-03. The data is a polygon shapefile that is used to show which areas of the region should be considered urbanized in nature when making decisions about federal aid roadways. However, the location of the line is not detailed enough to be used for determining urban or rural roadways if it coincides with the actual boundary line being placed on a roadway.

items.title: How do crashes impact vulnerable communities? StoryMap
items.description:
Crashes tend to happen at higher rates in communities that have high concentrations of poverty and people of color. Historically, these are the same communities that have been underrepresented in the planning process. Because these neighborhoods bear a disproportionate share of negative societal impacts, they are often referred to as “vulnerable communities”. The Metropolitan Transportation Plan identifies these communities in terms of a regional Environmental Justice (EJ) index.  

See the map below showing fatal crashes with MRCOG's Environmental Justice (EJ) Index. The EJ Index combines the percentage of households living in poverty with the percentage of persons of color in a census tract to create an "EJ score" between 2 and 10. The higher the score, the more vulnerable the community, represented by darker shades in the map below.

items.title: HFIN All Modes Web Map 2017_ 2021
items.description:
The High Fatal & Injury Network (HFIN)  

The HFIN was developed to help target funding to the most dangerous streets and intersections and get the biggest bang for our "safety buck".   

The HFIN symbolizes segments with high levels of fatal and injury crashes per mile, and fatal and injury intersection crash rates (divided by approaching traffic) for every major road (arterials and collectors) in the region.   

The HFIN score is derived from summing the number of fatal and injury crashes on every link and then dividing that number by the length of the link in miles. The number of fatal crashes on each link is multiplied by 2 to give them greater significance than injury crashes.  

The formula for the HFIN Score for any given link is: (fatal crashes *2) + injury crashes/ length of link in miles.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN Score of 319.8 or higher (2 times the regional mean or higher) make up only 2.5% of the major roadway network. However, 26% of the fatalities and 40% of the injury crashes happened on these roadways between 2017 and 2021.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN score of 159.9 or higher (simply above the regional mean) make up only 8% of the major roadways, but contain 47% of the fatal crashes and 64% of the injury crashes. 

Interstates were not included because they are maintained and operated by the NMDOT. For more about NMDOT safety initiatives check out their Planning Division.

items.name: Household_Poverty___Bernalillo_County___2014_and_2019
items.title: Household Poverty _ Bernalillo County _ 2014 and 2019
items.description:
MRMPO shares these layers solely for the purpose of visualizing basic poverty information based on US Census Bureau geographies and statistics.

Tract boundaries are from 2019 Tiger state geodatabase for New Mexico (35), selected for Bernalillo County (001).
Poverty data (2015-2019) is from American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year data, table B17017, 2019.
Poverty data (2010-2014) is from American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year data, table B17017, 2014.
Each layer has an added field (HHPovPerc) with a calculated percentage of households per tract with income below the national poverty level. The calculation used was as follows: 100 * B17017_002E / B17017_001E, or 100 times the quotient of estimated households with income below poverty level divided by estimated total households. Calculations were done per tract. Field names are defined in the "Table Shells" data dictionaries linked below.

Additional information:
Tiger geodatabases: https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/tiger-geodatabase-file.html
American community survey and other Census data: https://data.census.gov/cedsci/ 
2019 Table shells: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/technical-documentation/table-shells.2019.html
2014 Table shells: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/technical-documentation/table-shells.2014.html
items.snippet: Census tracts (2019) for Bernalillo County joined to ACS table B17017 (poverty by household). One sublayer uses 2014 5-year data (2010-2014) and one sublayer uses 2019 5-year data (2015-2019).

items.title: AMPA Historically Disadvantaged Communities
items.description:
"The Biden-Harris Administration created the Justice40 Initiative to confront and address decades of underinvestment in disadvantaged communities. The initiative will bring resources to communities most impacted by climate change, pollution, and environmental hazards."

In February 2022 the White House Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) released The Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool (CEJST in beta form.  The tool aims to help Federal agencies identify disadvantaged communities (DACs) that are marginalized, underserved, and overburdened by pollution as part of the Justice40 Initiative.  While CEJST is still in beta, the Department is using an interim definition to identify disadvantaged communities for Justice40-covered programs, consistent with Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance and relevant statutory authorities. DOT is using this interim definition to ask applicants to Justice40-covered programs to identify how their projects benefit DACs.

USDOT’s interim definition of DACs includes (a) certain qualifying census tracts, (b) any Tribal land, or (c) any territory or possession of the United States. USDOT has provided a mapping tool to assist applicants in identifying whether a project is located in a Disadvantaged Community, available at Transportation Disadvantaged Census Tracts.  

A shapefile of the geospatial data is available, and this map is made from an export from that shapefile to identify DACs within the Albuquerque Metro Planning Area.  To learn more about Justice40 covered funding opportunities and the USDOT's implementation efforts, see: https://www.transportation.gov/equity-Justice40

items.title: MRCOG Vulnerability Indices 2016-2020
items.description:
Based on the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) of the Center for Disease Control and Prevention, the MRMPO Vulnerability Index (MVI) score provides an indicator of the relative ability of communities to survive and thrive when confronted by external stresses on human health, such as exposure to environmental pollution and the hazards associated with climate change. In additional to the demographic factors included in the SVI methodology,* the MVI adds measures of gender, ethnic and national origin. 

Using 2016-2020 census American Community Survey (ACS) data, tract-level demographic information is provided in a pop-up window by clicking on the map, and percent ranked (percentile) variables are combined into one percentile value representing a comparative measure of resident population vulnerability relative to other tracts in the regional or metropolitan area.

An additional score is provided as an indication of the residential concentration of those populations of special concern for environmental justice considerations - "low-income and minority" populations, or persons of color, of Hispanic/Latine ethnicity, and those with annual incomes below the federal poverty level.

*Demographic indicators of social vulnerability:

  • Socioeconomic Status
    • Below 150% Poverty
    • Unemployed
    • Housing Cost Burden
    • No High School Diploma
    • No Health Insurance
  • Household Characteristics
    • Aged 65 & Older
    • Aged 17 & Younger
    • Civilian with a Disability
    • Single-Parent Households
    • English Language Proficiency
  • Racial & Ethnic Minority Status
    • Hispanic or Latino (of any race); Black and African American; American Indian and Alaska Native; Asian; Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander; Two or More Races; Other Races
  • Housing Type & Transportation
    • Multi-Unit Structures
    • Mobile Homes
    • Crowding
    • No Vehicle
    • Group Quarters
items.snippet: Map visualizing social vulnerability indices of the Albuquerque Metro and Regional Planning Areas, shaded to represent the relative concentration of populations of concern for equity and protection from harm. Among other contributing factors*, vulnerable populations include children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities.

items.title: MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer
items.description:
MRCOG collects traffic counts at all major roads in Bernalillo, Valencia, Torrance, Sandoval, and southern Santa Fe counties. The resulting traffic data is used to support local, state, and federal transportation planning activities and to produce annual Traffic Flow Maps for the entire areas within the boundaries of the MRCOG planning area (including both metropolitan and rural areas; https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/623/Traffic-Flow-Maps-and-Busiest-Intersecti). 

Most traffic counts are performed using portable traffic monitoring devices with rubber tubes that stretch across the roadway (pneumonic tube counters). 

Additional traffic data is collected by the New Mexico Department of Transportation through a series of permanent count stations on Interstates and certain arterials. These locations provide continuous data-reporting which is also used for seasonal factoring for annualized data averaging from the short-term counts as noted above. 

All major roads functionally-classified as collectors or higher are counted on a periodic schedule every three years. Traffic monitoring devices are placed at a location for 48 hours to produce average daily and peak period traffic volume levels, as well as directional split values (the percentage of travel in each direction for the day or peak period). Devices are set out on Mondays or Tuesdays and picked up on Wednesdays or Thursdays. Growth factors are applied in the intervening years and seasonal factors are applied based on the time of year the count was taken to generate yearly data.

For more information, please visit our website: https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/285/Traffic-Monitoring.

Problems viewing the app? Please contact gis@mrcog-nm.gov.
items.snippet: A web app for viewing traffic counts in the MRCOG region. Counts are presented by roadway section and by approximate count locations. Features include tabular data exports and basic map exports.
items.licenseInfo:
This app, and all maps and data contained within, are intended for general reference purposes only.

Additional statistical information is available upon request. MRMPO occasionally collects traffic data for special studies, requested by our member agencies. Additionally, there are summary reports that include vehicle classification, Vehicle Hours Traveled (VHT) and Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) for the region. For more information, please visit our website: https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/285/Traffic-Monitoring.

items.title: High Fatal and Injury Network (HFIN)-Paul
items.description: This map includes data from 2011 to 2015 in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area. The data in this map is specifically fatal and injury crashes. The map depicts roadway segments where the crashes per mile are above the mean. The HFIN includes only those that are 2x above the mean. Some acronyms are used including LU = Large Urban area, SU = Small Urban area, and RU = Rural area. This map was created by the Mid Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO). These are created based on federal funding categories. Please contact Caeri Thomas at cthomas@mrcog-nm.gov with any questions.
items.snippet: Shows fatal and injury crashes for the region above the mean. Also includes total pedestrian crashes above the mean.
items.licenseInfo:
•This is a sample of the data – it may not contain all crashes that have happened.
•There are also crashes that are never reported.
•The crash data is provided by University of New Mexico Geospatial Population Studies department, whose staff geocode the crash record data. Complete accuracy of geographic coordinate is not guaranteed.
•The data is acquired and reviewed by the New Mexico Department of Transportation’s (NMDOT) Traffic Safety Bureau from police records across the State of New Mexico.
•A crash must involve at least one motor vehicle, occur on a public roadway, and result in at least $500 of property damage or personal injury.
•This crash data, along with Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization’s major roads street network and traffic counts data, allow for calculating crash rates for the region.
•Fatality and injury crashes are the focus of this plan because these crashes are associated with the greatest human and financial cost to the public.

items.title: Tribal_Areas_BIA_LAR_MRCOG
items.description:
The purpose of the American Indian and Alaska Native Land Area Representation (AIAN-LAR) Geographic Information System (GIS) dataset is to depict the external extent of federal Indian reservations and the external extent of associated land held in “trust” by the United States, “restricted fee” or “mixed ownership” status for federally recognized tribes and individual Indians. This dataset includes other land area types such as Public Domain Allotments, Dependent Indian Communities and Homesteads.

This GIS Dataset is prepared strictly for illustrative and reference purposes only and should not be used, and is not intended for legal, survey, engineering or navigation purposes.

No warranty is made by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) for the use of the data for purposes not intended by the BIA. This GIS Dataset may contain errors. There is no impact on the legal status of the land areas depicted herein and no impact on land ownership. No legal inference can or should be made from the information in this GIS Dataset. The GIS Dataset is to be used solely for illustrative, reference and statistical purposes and may be used for government to government Tribal consultation.

Reservation boundary data is limited in authority to those areas where there has been settled Congressional definition or final judicial interpretation of the boundary. Absent settled Congressional definition or final judicial interpretation of a reservation boundary, the BIA recommends consultation with the appropriate Tribe and then the BIA to obtain interpretations of the reservation boundary.

The land areas and their representations are compilations defined by the official land title records of the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) which include treaties, statutes, Acts of Congress, agreements, executive orders, proclamations, deeds and other land title documents. The trust, restricted, and mixed ownership land area shown here, are suitable only for general spatial reference and do not represent the federal government’s position on the jurisdictional status of Indian country. Ownership and jurisdictional status is subject to change and must be verified with plat books, patents, and deeds in the appropriate federal and state offices.

Included in this dataset are the exterior extent of off reservation trust, restricted fee tracts and mixed tracts of land including Public Domain allotments, Dependent Indian Communities, Homesteads and government administered lands and those set aside for schools and dormitories. There are also land areas where there is more than one tribe having an interest in or authority over a tract of land but this information is not specified in the AIAN-LAR dataset. The dataset includes both surface and subsurface tracts of land (tribal and individually held) “off reservation” tracts and not simply off reservation “allotments” as land has in many cases been subsequently acquired in trust.

These data are public information and may be used by various organizations, agencies, units of government (i.e., Federal, state, county, and city), and other entities according to the restrictions on appropriate use. It is strongly recommended that these data be acquired directly from the BIA and not indirectly through some other source, which may have altered or integrated the data for another purpose for which they may not have been intended. Integrating land areas into another dataset and attempting to resolve boundary differences between other entities may produce inaccurate results. It is also strongly recommended that careful attention be paid to the content of the metadata file associated with these data. Users are cautioned that digital enlargement of these data to scales greater than those at which they were originally mapped can cause misinterpretation.

The BIA AIAN-LAR dataset’s spatial accuracy and attribute information are continuously being updated, improved and is used as the single authoritative land area boundary data for the BIA mission. These data are available through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, Office of Trust Services, Division of Land Titles and Records, Branch of Geospatial Support.

items.title: HFIN Bicyclists Web Map 2017_2021
items.description:
The High Fatal & Injury Network (HFIN)  

The HFIN was developed to help target funding to the most dangerous streets and intersections and get the biggest bang for our "safety buck".   

The HFIN symbolizes segments with high levels of fatal and injury crashes per mile, and fatal and injury intersection crash rates (divided by approaching traffic) for every major road (arterials and collectors) in the region.   

The HFIN score is derived from summing the number of fatal and injury crashes on every link and then dividing that number by the length of the link in miles. The number of fatal crashes on each link is multiplied by 2 to give them greater significance than injury crashes.  

The formula for the HFIN Score for any given link is: (fatal crashes *2) + injury crashes/ length of link in miles.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN Score of 319.8 or higher (2 times the regional mean or higher) make up only 2.5% of the major roadway network. However, 26% of the fatalities and 40% of the injury crashes happened on these roadways between 2017 and 2021.  

The HFIN links that have an HFIN score of 159.9 or higher (simply above the regional mean) make up only 8% of the major roadways, but contain 47% of the fatal crashes and 64% of the injury crashes. 

Interstates were not included because they are maintained and operated by the NMDOT. For more about NMDOT safety initiatives check out their Planning Division.

items.title: MRMPO Regional Data Viewer v1.0
items.description:
An interactive web mapping application featuring a variety of transportation planning datasets maintained by the Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO) in Albuquerque, NM, USA. 

The layers in this map are consistent with the goals of Connections 2040 long-range Metropolitan Transportation Plan (MTP). They include transportation data such as roadway congestion, bike facilities, and crash data, as well as land use data such as major Activity Centers. Data shown in this viewer may be incorporated into the ongoing update of the Project Prioritization Process (PPP) that will support the 2024 - 2029 Transportation Improvement Plan (TIP). The 2024 - 2029 TIP begins development in the fall of 2022.

Please note that in the development of the MTP, 2016 was considered the base year (2012 for activity density) and data for base years are estimates, while data for the 2040 horizon year are projections.

https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/233/Metropolitan-Planning-Organization

Version 1.0 was published in October 2021.

Problems viewing the map? Please contact GIS@mrcog-nm.gov.

items.title: Disadvantaged Census Tracts of USDOT Screening Tool
items.description:
"The Biden-Harris Administration created the Justice40 Initiative to confront and address decades of underinvestment in disadvantaged communities. The initiative will bring resources to communities most impacted by climate change, pollution, and environmental hazards."

In February 2022 the White House Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) released The Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool (CEJST in beta form.  The tool aims to help Federal agencies identify disadvantaged communities (DACs) that are marginalized, underserved, and overburdened by pollution as part of the Justice40 Initiative.  While CEJST is still in beta, the Department is using an interim definition to identify disadvantaged communities for Justice40-covered programs, consistent with Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance and relevant statutory authorities. DOT is using this interim definition to ask applicants to Justice40-covered programs to identify how their projects benefit DACs.

Consistent with OMB’s Interim Guidance for the Justice40 Initiative, DOT’s interim definition of DACs includes (a) certain qualifying census tracts, (b) any Tribal land, or (c) any territory or possession of the United States. DOT has provided a mapping tool to assist applicants in identifying whether a project is located in a Disadvantaged Community, available at Transportation Disadvantaged Census Tracts (https://usdot.maps.arcgis.com/apps/dashboards/d6f90dfcc8b44525b04c7ce748a3674a).  

A shapefile of the geospatial data is available, and this layer is an export from the shapefile for tracts within the Albuquerque Metro Planning Area.  To learn more about Justice40 covered funding opportunities and the USDOT's implementation efforts, see: https://www.transportation.gov/equity-Justice40
items.snippet: Export from the USDOT screening tool for identifying tracts where disadvantaged communities within the Albuquerque Metro Planning Area may benefit from Justice40 covered programs and funding opportunities.

items.title: MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer Map
items.description:
This map is intended for viewing in the MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer app: https://arcg.is/1XXbO51.

MRCOG collects traffic counts at all major roads in Bernalillo, Valencia, Torrance, Sandoval, and southern Santa Fe counties. The resulting traffic data is used to support local, state, and federal transportation planning activities and to produce annual Traffic Flow Maps for the entire areas within the boundaries of the MRCOG planning area (including both metropolitan and rural areas; https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/623/Traffic-Flow-Maps-and-Busiest-Intersecti). 

Most traffic counts are performed using portable traffic monitoring devices with rubber tubes that stretch across the roadway (pneumonic tube counters). 

Additional traffic data is collected by the New Mexico Department of Transportation through a series of permanent count stations on Interstates and certain arterials. These locations provide continuous data-reporting which is also used for seasonal factoring for annualized data averaging from the short-term counts as noted above. 

All major roads functionally-classified as collectors or higher are counted on a periodic schedule every three years. Traffic monitoring devices are placed at a location for 48 hours to produce average daily and peak period traffic volume levels, as well as directional split values (the percentage of travel in each direction for the day or peak period). Devices are set out on Mondays or Tuesdays and picked up on Wednesdays or Thursdays. Growth factors are applied in the intervening years and seasonal factors are applied based on the time of year the count was taken to generate yearly data.

For more information, please visit our website: https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/285/Traffic-Monitoring.

Problems viewing the app? Please contact gis@mrcog-nm.gov.
items.snippet: This map is intended for viewing in the MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer app: https://arcg.is/1XXbO51. A web map for viewing traffic counts in the MRCOG region. Counts are presented by roadway section and by approximate count locations. Features include tabular data exports and basic map exports.
items.licenseInfo:
This map is intended for viewing in the MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer app: https://arcg.is/1XXbO51. This map and data contained within are intended for general reference purposes only.

Additional statistical information is available upon request. MRMPO occasionally collects traffic data for special studies, requested by our member agencies. Additionally, there are summary reports that include vehicle classification, Vehicle Hours Traveled (VHT) and Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) for the region. For more information, please visit our website: https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/285/Traffic-Monitoring.

items.title: MRCOG Vulnerability Indices 2016-2020
items.description:
Based on the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) of the Center for DiseaseControl and Prevention, the MRMPO Vulnerability Index (MVI) score provides an indicator of the relative ability of communities to survive and thrive when confronted by external stresses on human health, such as exposure to environmental pollution and the hazards associated with climate change. In addition to the demographic factors included in the SVI methodology,* the MVI adds measures of gender, ethnic and national origin. 

Using 2016-2020 census American Community Survey (ACS) data, tract-level demographic information is provided in a pop-up window by clicking on the map, and percent ranked (percentile) variables are combined into one percentile value representing a comparative measure of resident population vulnerability relative to other tracts in the regional or metropolitan area.

An additional score is provided as an indication of the residential concentration of those populations of special concern for environmental justice considerations - "low-income and minority" populations, or persons of color, of Hispanic/Latine ethnicity, and those with annual incomes below the federal poverty level.

*Demographic indicators of social vulnerability:

  • Socioeconomic Status
    • Below 150% Poverty
    • Unemployed
    • Housing Cost Burden
    • No High School Diploma
    • No Health Insurance
  • Household Characteristics
    • Aged 65 & Older
    • Aged 17 & Younger
    • Civilian with a Disability
    • Single-Parent Households
    • English Language Proficiency
  • Racial & Ethnic Minority Status
    • Hispanic or Latino (of any race); Black and African American; American Indian and Alaska Native; Asian; Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander; Two or More Races; Other Races
  • Housing Type & Transportation
    • Multi-Unit Structures
    • Mobile Homes
    • Crowding
    • No Vehicle
    • Group Quarters
items.snippet: Map visualizing social vulnerability indices of the Albuquerque Metro and Regional Planning Areas, shaded to represent the relative concentration of populations of concern for equity and protection from harm. Among other contributing factors*, vulnerable populations include children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities.

items.title: High Fatal and Injury Network (HFIN)
items.description: This map includes data from 2011 to 2015 in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area. The data in this map is specifically fatal and injury crashes. The map depicts roadway segments where the crashes per mile are above the mean. The HFIN includes only those that are 2x above the mean. Some acronyms are used including LU = Large Urban area, SU = Small Urban area, and RU = Rural area. This map was created by the Mid Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO). These are created based on federal funding categories. Please contact Caeri Thomas at cthomas@mrcog-nm.gov with any questions.
items.snippet: Shows fatal and injury crashes for the region above the mean. Also includes total pedestrian crashes above the mean.
items.licenseInfo:
•This is a sample of the data – it may not contain all crashes that have happened.
•There are also crashes that are never reported.
•The crash data is provided by University of New Mexico Geospatial Population Studies department, whose staff geocode the crash record data. Complete accuracy of geographic coordinate is not guaranteed.
•The data is acquired and reviewed by the New Mexico Department of Transportation’s (NMDOT) Traffic Safety Bureau from police records across the State of New Mexico.
•A crash must involve at least one motor vehicle, occur on a public roadway, and result in at least $500 of property damage or personal injury.
•This crash data, along with Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization’s major roads street network and traffic counts data, allow for calculating crash rates for the region.
•Fatality and injury crashes are the focus of this plan because these crashes are associated with the greatest human and financial cost to the public.

items.title: fiber damages MRCOG area
items.description:
Dates for this ticket are between July 14th and October 15th, 2025. Ticket extent were all tickets within the boudaries of Albuquerque, Los Ranchos, Corrales, Rio Rancho, and Kirtland Air Force Base.

Fields for this data are:
ticketid | ticket number | starting date | creation tme | work starting time | ticket type | work type | Excavator Name | Excavator type | Facility damaged | Investigation Status | related cases | PRC Investigator Assigned | Violation | Previously called one call

Geospatial data along with ticket id, number, stat date, creation time, work starting time, ticket type, and work type, for this layer was taken from NM811 call center ticket buffers.
Excavator information including: excavator name, excavator type, and facility damaged were taken from the NM811 report: Damage Tickets DR Expanded. The facility damaged was anonimyzed by assigning a value of either {Power, Gas, Communications, Potable Water, Reclaimed Water, Sewer} based on the APWA Uniform Color Code of the markings left by the facility operator's line locators.
Investigation information including: Investigation Status, Related Caseds, PRC Investigator Assigned, Violation, and Previously called one call, were taken from the Irth Utilisphere Damage reporting software used by the Pipeline Safety Bureau.

This showed 425 features for the study area in the study time frame, with the following violations recorded:

  • 1 time a facility operator failed to locate or clear within the advanced notice period
  • 39 times an excavator used mechincal excavation means within the 18" tolerance zone
  • 1 time an excavator failed to maintain marks
  • 5times an excavator failed to make a locate request
  • 69 times facility operators failed to properly mark their facilities
  • 2 times damages were unneccesarily reported
  • 165 times damages were not the result of a violation of the safe digging law
  • 143 reports are still under investigation

items.title: MRCOG_Traffic_Count_Segments
items.description:
This layer is intended for viewing in the MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer app: https://arcg.is/1XXbO51.

MRCOG (Mid-Region Council of Governments; Albuquerque, New Mexico) counts traffic on major roads. Major roads are defined by functional classification and comprise urban minor collectors and above (including rural major collectors and above). Traffic counts are shown by road segment (also called edges or links) - a contiguous section of road from one major intersection to the next. Counts are calculated for both annual average daily traffic (ADT) and annual average weekday traffic (AWDT).

MRCOG collects traffic counts at all major roads in Bernalillo, Valencia, Torrance, Sandoval, and southern Santa Fe counties. The resulting traffic data is used to support local, state, and federal transportation planning activities and to produce annual Traffic Flow Maps for the entire areas within the boundaries of the MRCOG planning area (including both metropolitan and rural areas; https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/623/Traffic-Flow-Maps-and-Busiest-Intersecti).
items.snippet: This layer is intended for viewing in the MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer app: https://arcg.is/1XXbO51. Traffic counts (ADT and AWDT) for 2007-2020 in the MRCOG region.
items.licenseInfo:
This layer is intended for viewing in the MRCOG Traffic Counts Viewer app: https://arcg.is/1XXbO51. The data contained within are intended for general reference purposes only.

Additional statistical information is available upon request. MRMPO occasionally collects traffic data for special studies, requested by our member agencies. Additionally, there are summary reports that include vehicle classification, Vehicle Hours Traveled (VHT) and Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) for the region. For more information, please visit our website: https://www.mrcog-nm.gov/285/Traffic-Monitoring.

items.name: Oregon_MPO_PlaceTypes.sd
items.title: Oregon_MPO_PlaceTypes
items.description:
Area Type (or Regional Role) describes the inter-dependencies of each neighborhood compared to the rest of the region, e.g. how centered is it to jobs in the region. The Area Type is a measured by the accessibility to Destinations (jobs accessible from TAZ), Density (jobs and households per acre), and walkable street Design (multi-modal network links). Development Type (or Neighborhood Character) is used to describe the physical characteristics of each neigborhood in isolation. Development Type is determined by the Density (jobs and households per acre), walkable street Design (multi-modal network links), land-use Diversity (ratio of jobs to households), and presence of transit (service level) within each neighborhood district. More informatin on the Place Types can be found at:
 http://www.oregon.gov/ODOT/TD/TP/ORPlaceTypes/PlaceType_Flyer.pdf
Levels: 
H - High
M - Medium
L - Low
VL - Very Low
items.snippet: In order to better understand land use and transportation interactions and to make more informed policy decisions, neighborhood characteristics can be analyzed by the role that they play in the region; a more comprehensive view than parcel changes, but more specific than zoning and comprehensive plans. Place Types are data-driven ways to define and visualize the many aspects of land use-transportation interactions embodied in our land use plans.  Characteristics of the bult environmen influence the transportation choices that individuals make, and ultimately affect the overall amount of vehicle travel in the region. By comparing the existing built environment characteristics to what is expected to occur in the future, we are able to explore how changes to the built environment can affect travel.
items.licenseInfo: For planning and informative purposes only.

items.title: Long Range Roadway System 2040
items.description:
The Long Range Roadway System (LRRS) provides future recommended roadways and their regional role. This system should be viewed as an aspiration network. That is, the map demonstrates how the region's roadways are envisioned to function as a network with some roads closer to their desired functionality than others. This system also identify future basic network connectivity needs. 

 

The Long Range Roadway System does not provide current functional classification that determines if the roadway is eligible for federal funds. Instead, the LRRS, builds upon the functional classification categories by considering the character of the roadway and the role it plays in the regional network. The main distinction is differentiating principle arterials into two groups: regional and community. Regional principle arterials are primarily for travel across the region with high levels of access management, whereas trips on community principle arterials are shorter and tend to be be to destinations with direct access off the arterial.  
 

Future roadways that are beyond the 2040 time frame are highlighted in grey. 
 
This map is created and updated by the Mid-Region Council of Governments Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO). It is updated concurrently with the Metropolitan Transportation Plan (MTP).

items.title: MRMPO Pedestrian Composite Index (PCI) App
items.description:
The Pedestrian Composite Index (PCI) is a tool for targeting improvements to pedestrian facilities in places where pedestrian activity is expected to be greatest. Improving walkability and safety in these locations should be prioritized if suitable facilities do not already exist. The National Association of City Transportation Officials (NACTO) recommends wider sidewalks with buffers or planter strips and safer roadway crossings that are closer together.

In the absence of comprehensive sidewalk condition data and pedestrian traffic counts, the PCI projects pedestrian activity on a given street segment based on conditions that potentially generate or attract pedestrian travel.

The Index includes factors such as:
 - proximity to schools, bus stops, parks, and community centers;
 - proximity to higher density areas of jobs and housing;
 - density of roadway connections;
 - transit use; and
 - availability of personal vehicles.

Due to the high pedestrian fatality rates in our region, it is imperative that we work on bringing different methods, data, partners, and approaches together to ensure the pedestrian network and pedestrian safety improve over time.

items.title: Roadway Bicycle Guidelines (2013)
items.description:
Welcome to NMDOT's
Roadway Bicycle Guideline
Map

The New Mexico Department of Transportation's State Bicycle Guideline Map is provided to assist cyclists in choosing preferred routes when bicycling through New Mexico. The map shows usable shoulder width estimates, presence of rumble strips, and segments of steep grade for all NMDOT-owned roads in New Mexico. The map also includes a more detailed layer of bicycle facilities in the Albuquerque area, provided by the Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO).

Usable shoulder width estimates were adjusted shoulder data depending on the presence of rumble strips, guardrails or other adjacent barriers. Traffic volumes are derived from averages, and you may experience more or less traffic than displayed on the map. When bicycling throughout New Mexico, please make sure to plan accordingly. Call ahead to communities and potential service providers to verify that your destination has the services you need or want. Some areas of the state are quite remote and uninhabited. While these are some of the very qualities that draw visitors to New Mexico, please note that some communities displayed on our map may not have the services you expect. Further, all information contained on this map is subject to change. We hope you enjoy your bicycling trips throughout the Land of Enchantment! Whether you are climbing mountain passes or enjoying the long open road, our wonderful climate, incomparable vistas, and unique history are sure to provide you with a memorable experience.

In case of Emergency, call 911. New Mexico Roads provides information on current roadway conditions, including construction. Please call 511 or visit NMRoads.com for more information. Please read the Notice of Disclaimer under Access and Use Constraints.

This map includes a layer with bicycle facility data from the Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO) showing bikeway facilities in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area (AMPA) which includes Bernalillo County, Valencia County, and part of Sandoval County.

MRMPO defines their bicycle facility data terms as follows:
•    BIKE LANE = division of roadway marked off with painted lines for use by bicyclists.
•    BIKE ROUTE = a roadway with appropriate direction and informational signing for bicyclists, usually on low-speed, low-traffic streets.
•    BIKE BOULEVARD = a bike route that is designed to prioritize bicycle through movement while also maintaining local access for motor vehicles. Often bicycle boulevards include a variety of traffic calming measures. They are also known as Neighborhood Greenways.
•    MULTI-USE TRAIL = a pathway that is physically separated from the roadway for pedestrians, bicyclists, and wheelchair users.

Most trails are designed for two-way traffic. For questions related to MRMPO data specifically, please contact Tara Cok at the Mid-Region Council of Governments (MRCOG). MRCOG phone number: (505) 247-1750.

For bicycle maps and resources from various communities in New Mexico, please follow the links below:

•    Albuquerque region bike map
•    Farmington city bike map
•    Santa Fe region bike map

items.title: Road Diets in the Albuquerque Region
items.description: This map includes data from 2011 to 2015 in the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area. The data in this map is specifically fatal and injury crashes. The map depicts roadway segments where the crashes per mile are above the mean. The HFIN includes only those that are 2x above the mean. Some acronyms are used including LU = Large Urban area, SU = Small Urban area, and RU = Rural area. This map was created by the Mid Region Metropolitan Planning Organization (MRMPO). These are created based on federal funding categories. Please contact Caeri Thomas at cthomas@mrcog-nm.gov with any questions.
items.snippet: Shows the high fatal and injury network plus potential road diet candidates based on traffic volume and number of lanes.
items.licenseInfo:
•This is a sample of the data – it may not contain all crashes that have happened.
•There are also crashes that are never reported.
•The crash data is provided by University of New Mexico Geospatial Population Studies department, whose staff geocode the crash record data. Complete accuracy of geographic coordinate is not guaranteed.
•The data is acquired and reviewed by the New Mexico Department of Transportation’s (NMDOT) Traffic Safety Bureau from police records across the State of New Mexico.
•A crash must involve at least one motor vehicle, occur on a public roadway, and result in at least $500 of property damage or personal injury.
•This crash data, along with Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization’s major roads street network and traffic counts data, allow for calculating crash rates for the region.
•Fatality and injury crashes are the focus of this plan because these crashes are associated with the greatest human and financial cost to the public.

items.description: The boundary of the Albuquerque Metropolitan Planning Area (AMPA) was adopted in 2012 by the Metropolitan Transportation Board of the Mid-Region Council of Governments of New Mexico through resolution R-12-13 MTB. The 2012 boundary expanded the AMPA to include all of Valencia County, Bernalillo County, and the southeastern portion of Sandoval County. Metropolitan Planning Organizations (MPOs) are required by federal law for all urbanized areas with populations greater than 50,000. MPO's are responsible for carrying out metropolitan transportation plans and programs. The MPO for the AMPA is the Mid-Region Metropolitan Planning Organization. The Metropolitan Transportation Board, composed of local elected leaders, sets policy for transportation issues in the urban area.

The following statistics were developed for areas within city limits and within 1/2 mile of each ART station, including a proposed station at San Pedro Dr. and Central Ave. (see map Below).  The U.S. Census Bureau 2014 American Community Survey 5-year estimates at the block group level was the original data source, with the exception of ‘Total Employment,’ which came from the Mid-Region Council of Governments 2012 Socioeconomic dataset at the level of Data Analysis Sub Zone (DASZ).  Statistics were generated by summarizing census block group data (or DASZ) by station based on the proportionate area of the block group (or DASZ) that falls within the 1/2 mile station area buffer.

items.title: Albuquerque_MRCOG_Smoothed_Urban_Area_2013
items.description: The Albuquerque Smoothed Out Urbanized Area was developed based on input from local municipalities to determine the best way to smooth out the Census-designated Urbanized Area for Albuquerque, New Mexico for transportation planning purposed. The Albuquerque Smoothed Out Urbanized Area was approved by the Metropolitan Transportation Board of the Mid-Region Council of Governments of New Mexico in 2013 through resolution R-13-03. The data is a polygon shapefile that is used to show which areas of the region should be considered urbanized in nature when making decisions about federal aid roadways. However, the location of the line is not detailed enough to be used for determining urban or rural roadways if it coincides with the actual boundary line being placed on a roadway.
items.snippet: The Albuquerque Smoothed Out Urbanized Area determines which areas in and nearby the Census-designated Urbanized Area for Albuquerque, New Mexico are considered "large urban" for transportation planning purposes.
